extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism students, researchers, and journalism practitioners interested in television news production and critique
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation framework and index of concepts for analyzing television (and broadcast) news: audience factors, news values, institutional pressures, format and production considerations, and ethical/professional norms that shape story selection and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: audience considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience considerations (defined) — factors such as balance, boredom, expert vs. lay audiences, financial considerations, multiperspectival needs, panic/protective responses, versus source considerations; story importance, interest, length, repetition, and story opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use audience characteristics (size, regularity, attentiveness) and preferences to shape story selection, length, mix, and presentation; weigh audience fears/needs and avoid assuming a homogeneous audience. Beware over-serving a narrow demographic or pandering to protective/panic responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: audience size/regularity/enlargement
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience enlargement: considerations of audience size and regularity (e.g., growth in television ownership) and cultural democratization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether format/content changes increase or repel regular viewership; consider how format changes (magazine segments, anchor changes) affect audience composition and size.

rubrics_metrics.name: audience research and feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience research on attentiveness/regularity and informal/formal audience feedback (mail, types of feedback, conservative vs. other responses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate audience research to inform news policy and programming, but interpret feedback cautiously (distinguish crank mail from representative responses); use feedback as one input among editorial and professional criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: audience images and audience-journalist relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: How journalists imagine their audience (audience images) and the audience–journalist relationship (including fear of audiences and journalists as representatives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly consider the constructed image of the audience when making editorial decisions; avoid letting stereotyped audience images unduly constrain story choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: balance and balance considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance — demographic, geographical, political, racial, religious, sexual balance; story mixture and balance in cover/back-of-book placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for multiperspectival and demographic balance in story selection and placement; balance should be weighed against newsworthiness and factuality, not used as a pretext for false equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: objectivity and detachment
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectivity (including notions such as 'detachment' and 'objectivity as strategic ritual').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain professional norms of factual accuracy and impartial presentation while recognizing objectivity is practiced and negotiated; document methods and separate facts from analysis to support credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Fairness as an editorial criterion and function of editors/reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure fair treatment of subjects and viewpoints, use fairness doctrine/history as context; fairness should guide sourcing, representation, and opportunity to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Credibility of the news organization and journalists — includes maintaining credibility vis-à-vis audiences and as influenced by objectivity and self-censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize accurate sourcing and transparent methods; guard credibility against commercial or political pressures that could erode public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: enduring values / news values
rubrics_metrics.description: Enduring values and news values (defined as values used to judge news: e.g., democracy, business/responsible capitalism, national values).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply consistent normative values when judging importance and relevance of stories; be aware of how these values interact with institutional incentives and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: story selection / decision-making criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision-making criteria for story selection: importance, interest, anticipated stories, timing, novelty, and placement (cover stories/back-of-book).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate stories on multiple axes (importance, interest, timeliness, novelty); use editorial processes (beats, editors, executive producers) to adjudicate competing claims to coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: story importance vs. story interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between story importance (public significance) and story interest (audience appeal/interest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid privileging interest or entertainment value over civic importance; where tension exists, be transparent about editorial choices and rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: story freshness/novelty/fresh news
rubrics_metrics.description: Fresh news, novelty and gee-whiz stories — the value placed on newness and novelty in story selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance novelty with depth; avoid repetitive 'gee-whiz' coverage that crowds out important but less sensational topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: story length and repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Considerations of story length and story repetition (how long stories run and how often they are repeated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine appropriate length according to complexity and audience attention; avoid unnecessary repetition that breeds boredom but use repetition strategically for ongoing developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: format considerations and format change
rubrics_metrics.description: Format considerations (television vs. magazine format, format change, format rut, novelty, technology effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how format (e.g., magazine segments, anchor-driven shows) shapes story selection and presentation; watch for format rut and pursue innovation when it enhances coverage quality without sacrificing depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: anchorpersons and anchorman power/role
rubrics_metrics.description: Role and power of anchorpersons (audience relationships, commentary, eliminating role, format rut, influence on ratings and stories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how anchors' opinions, persona, and status affect framing and selection; manage anchor influence to preserve editorial integrity and avoid personality-driven distortion.

rubrics_metrics.name: competition and competitive considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Competition (internal and external), competitive pressures on cover stories, commercial competition, and role of leading newspapers as competitors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use competition as a quality control mechanism but guard against chase journalism and copying that undermines diversity of coverage; recognize commercial competition may influence editorial priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: commercial considerations and advertiser/affiliate pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial considerations (budgets, income, cost-cutting) and commercial pressures from advertisers and affiliate stations that shape news content and documentary censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and manage conflicts of interest; develop policies to insulate editorial judgment from advertiser or affiliate pressure and to disclose potential influences when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: professional autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional autonomy of journalists and news organizations — freedom to pursue stories independently from owners/advertisers/government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect editorial independence through institutional safeguards, clear editorial policy, and transparency about constraints or pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: censorship and self-censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Censorship: formal and informal (refusing access, chilling effect, censorship of documentaries, extent of censorship), and self-censorship by beat reporters and organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be vigilant about both overt censorship and more subtle chilling effects; document denials of access and consider ethical responses to pressure to withhold information.

rubrics_metrics.name: sources and source relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Source relations (beat reporters, source access, co-optation, sources such as CIA/FBI/government/leaks) and the power dynamics between reporters and sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize diverse sourcing, guard against co-optation, verify leaked and official information, and maintain transparency about source relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: investigative reporting / exposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Value and function of exposes and investigative reporting (e.g., Watergate, Selling of the Pentagon) and their vulnerability to pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support long-form and investigative work through resources and legal/ethical safeguards; consider the public interest in exposing wrongdoing despite potential risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: distortion (factual and framing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distortion: factual distortion, highlighting and exaggeration, and distortion through journalistic methods and selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor for exaggeration and framing effects; emphasize accuracy, context, and proportionality to avoid misleading audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: timeliness, breaking stories and deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Timeliness and breaking news (deadlines, freshness, timing of coverage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance speed with verification; avoid sacrificing accuracy for immediacy and establish protocols for live/breaking coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: representation and diversity (race/class/gender/ethnicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation of social groups (race, class, gender, ethnic groups), including coverage of blacks, black journalists, sex/gender issues, and class perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work actively to diversify sources and coverage; assess geographical, racial and class balance and correct persistent underrepresentation or stereotyped portrayals.

rubrics_metrics.name: multiperspectival news / multiperspectivalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiperspectival news — presenting multiple perspectives and avoiding single-story framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for multi-voiced reporting that reflects differing perspectives (political, class, demographic) while ensuring accuracy and relevance; avoid tokenism.

rubrics_metrics.name: gatekeeping / gatekeeper theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Gatekeeper functions in news selection and the role of editors/producers in deciding what becomes news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make gatekeeping criteria explicit where possible; audit decision-making to reduce bias and increase accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: efficiency and newsroom bureaucracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Efficiency in news production and the influence of bureaucracy on journalistic values and productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance operational efficiency with editorial quality; recognize how bureaucratic constraints can shape coverage and create perverse incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: research methods / content analysis as evaluation tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of content analysis, field work and other research methods to evaluate news content (sample design, content measures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ systematic content analysis and field research to measure bias, balance, topic distribution, and audience effects; ensure methodological transparency and appropriate samples.
